## Paired Means {#sec-paired-means}

```{r}
#| label: setup-3-3
#| include: false
source(if (file.exists("R/setup.R")) "R/setup.R" else "../R/setup.R")
stim <- read.csv(data_path("stimulus_spending.csv"))
train <- read.csv(data_path("training_wage.csv"))
before <- stim$before; after <- stim$after
```

### Learning Objectives

1. Recognize paired data from the way the data were collected.
2. Reduce paired data to differences $d$ and use the one-sample $t$ method on them.
3. Construct a CI and carry out a test for the mean difference $\mu_d$, by hand and from R.

### Concept

Data are **paired** when each observation in one group is matched with one
observation in the other group. Common designs:

- **Before and after:** the same households are measured before and after a policy.
- **Matched units:** the same products are priced at two shops; twin regions are compared.

Each pair gives one **difference** $d = x_1 - x_2$ (for example, after $-$ before).
The pairing removes the variation between units (rich and poor households
differ a lot, but each is compared with itself), so we analyse the
differences only. A paired test is a **one-sample $t$ test on $d$**
(Section 2.2) with $H_0: \mu_d = 0$.

::: {.callout-important icon=false}
## Paired or independent?

Decide from **how the data were collected**, not from the numbers:

- the same units measured twice, or units matched one-to-one → **paired**
- two separate random samples, with no link between a unit in one group and a unit in the other → **independent** (Section 3.5)

Paired samples always have the same size. Equal sample sizes alone do not make
the data paired.
:::

### Formulas and Conditions

**Conditions:** pairs are a random sample; the differences are approximately normal.

With $n$ pairs, $\bar{d}$ the mean and $s_d$ the standard deviation of the differences:

**$(1-\alpha)100\%$ confidence interval for $\mu_d$**
$$
\bar{d} \pm t_{1-\alpha/2,\,n-1}\,\frac{s_d}{\sqrt{n}}
$$

**Test statistic** for $H_0: \mu_d = 0$, with df $= n-1$
$$
t_{\text{cal}} = \frac{\bar{d}}{s_d/\sqrt{n}}
$$

**In R:** `t.test(after, before, paired = TRUE, alternative = ...)` uses
$d$ = after $-$ before (first argument minus second).

```{r}
#| label: ex-3-3
d <- after - before
n <- length(d); df_ <- n - 1
dbar <- mean(d); sd_ <- round(sd(d), 4)
se <- round(sd_ / sqrt(n), 4)
t_cal <- round(dbar / se, 3)
t975 <- crit_t(.975, df_); me <- t975 * se
og <- t.test(after, before, paired = TRUE, alternative = "greater")
o2 <- t.test(after, before, paired = TRUE)
```

### Example

**Example 3.3.1.** The government gave a cash transfer to low-income
households. A researcher recorded the monthly spending (baht) of `r n`
households in the month before and the month after the transfer. Did mean spending increase?

```{r}
#| label: tbl-stim
#| tbl-cap: "Monthly spending (baht) before and after the transfer, and the difference d = after - before"
knitr::kable(data.frame(Household = stim$household, Before = big(before, 0),
                        After = big(after, 0), d = big(d, 0)), align = "crrr")
```

(a) Construct a 95% confidence interval for the mean change in spending.
(b) At $\alpha$ = 0.05, test whether mean spending increased after the transfer.

::: {.callout-tip icon=false collapse=false}
## Solution

The same households are measured twice, so the data are paired. From the
differences: $n$ = `r n`, $\bar{d}$ = `r num(dbar)`, $s_d$ = `r num(sd_)`.
$$
\frac{s_d}{\sqrt{n}} = \frac{`r num(sd_)`}{\sqrt{`r n`}} = `r num(se)`
$$

**(a)** $t_{0.975,\,`r df_`} = `r fmt(t975, 3)`$:
$$
`r num(dbar)` \pm `r fmt(t975, 3)`(`r num(se)`) = `r num(dbar)` \pm `r num(me)`
$$
95% CI: (`r big(dbar - me)`, `r big(dbar + me)`)

We are 95% confident that the mean increase in monthly spending is between
`r big(dbar - me)` and `r big(dbar + me)` baht.

**(b)**

**Step 1: Hypotheses.** $H_0: \mu_d = 0$ $\quad H_1: \mu_d > 0$ (where $d$ = after $-$ before)

**Step 2: Level of significance.** $\alpha$ = 0.05

**Step 3: Test statistic.**
$$
t_{\text{cal}} = \frac{\bar{d}}{s_d/\sqrt{n}} = \frac{`r num(dbar)`}{`r num(se)`} = `r fmt(t_cal, 3)`
$$

**Step 4: p-value.** From the R output below, p-value = `r fmt(og$p.value, 4)`.

**Step 5: Decision and interpretation.** p-value = `r fmt(og$p.value, 4)` <
$\alpha$ = 0.05, so we reject $H_0$. That is, mean monthly spending increased
after the cash transfer at the 0.05 level of significance.
:::

### Reading R Output

```{r}
#| label: r-data-stim
#| echo: !expr show_code
#| code: !expr c(vec_code("before", before), vec_code("after", after))
```

```{r}
#| label: r-stim-greater
#| echo: !expr show_code
t.test(after, before, paired = TRUE, alternative = "greater")
```

`t = ` `r fmt(og$statistic, 3)` and `df = ` `r og$parameter` match the hand
calculation, and `mean difference` is $\bar{d}$ = `r num(dbar)`. For the 95% CI
we use the two-sided output:

```{r}
#| label: r-stim-two
#| echo: !expr show_code
t.test(after, before, paired = TRUE)
```

R gives (`r big(o2$conf.int[1])`, `r big(o2$conf.int[2])`). The hand
calculation gave (`r big(dbar - me)`, `r big(dbar + me)`). The small difference
comes from rounding: the table gives $t_{0.975,\,9}$ = `r fmt(t975, 3)`, while R uses
`r format(qt(.975, 9), digits = 7)`.

```{r}
#| label: yt-3-3
w_d <- train$after - train$before
w_n <- length(w_d); w_dbar <- round(mean(w_d), 4); w_sd <- round(sd(w_d), 4)
w_se <- round(w_sd / sqrt(w_n), 4); w_t <- round(w_dbar / w_se, 3)
wo <- t.test(train$after, train$before, paired = TRUE)
wage_after <- train$after; wage_before <- train$before
```

### Your Turn

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Your Turn 3.3.1

The daily wage (baht) of `r w_n` workers was recorded before and after a
training course. For $d$ = after $-$ before,
$\bar{d}$ = `r num(w_dbar)` and $s_d$ = `r num(w_sd)`.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-train
knitr::kable(data.frame(Worker = train$worker, Before = train$before, After = train$after,
                        d = w_d), align = "cccc")
```

(a) Calculate $t_{\text{cal}}$ by hand.
(b) Use the R output to test whether the training changed the mean daily wage at $\alpha$ = 0.05.
:::

```{r}
#| label: r-data-train
#| echo: !expr show_code
#| code: !expr c(vec_code("wage_before", train$before), vec_code("wage_after", train$after))
```

```{r}
#| label: r-yt-3-3
#| echo: !expr show_code
t.test(wage_after, wage_before, paired = TRUE)
```

::: {.workspace lines="14"}
:::

::: {.answer title="Your Turn 3.3.1"}
**(a)** $s_d/\sqrt{n} = `r num(w_sd)`/\sqrt{`r w_n`} = `r num(w_se)`$;
$t_{\text{cal}} = `r num(w_dbar)`/`r num(w_se)` = `r fmt(w_t, 3)`$ (R: `r fmt(wo$statistic, 3)`).

**(b)**

**Step 1.** $H_0: \mu_d = 0 \quad H_1: \mu_d \ne 0$

**Step 2.** $\alpha$ = 0.05

**Step 3.** $t_{\text{cal}} = `r fmt(wo$statistic, 3)`$, df = `r wo$parameter`

**Step 4.** p-value = `r fmt(wo$p.value, 4)`

**Step 5.** p-value = `r fmt(wo$p.value, 4)` $\ge$ $\alpha$ = 0.05, so we accept $H_0$.
That is, the training did not change the mean daily wage (the mean difference
is equal to 0) at the 0.05 level of significance.
:::

### Formula Summary

| | Formula |
|:---|:---|
| Differences | $d$ = first $-$ second for each pair; $\bar{d}$, $s_d$, $n$ pairs |
| $(1-\alpha)100\%$ CI for $\mu_d$ | $\bar{d} \pm t_{1-\alpha/2,\,n-1}\,s_d/\sqrt{n}$ |
| Test statistic | $t_{\text{cal}} = \dfrac{\bar{d}}{s_d/\sqrt{n}}$, df $= n-1$ |
| R | `t.test(x1, x2, paired = TRUE, alternative = ...)`, $d$ = `x1` $-$ `x2` |

```{r}
#| label: ex-3-3-exercises
shopA <- c(42, 118, 65, 89, 27, 154, 73, 36)
shopB <- c(45, 121, 64, 94, 29, 159, 77, 38)
eo <- t.test(shopA, shopB, paired = TRUE, alternative = "less")
```

### Exercises

**3.3.1** Paired or independent?

(a) The household income of 50 families is recorded in 2024 and again in 2025.
(b) The wages of 40 randomly chosen workers in Chiang Mai are compared with the wages of 40 randomly chosen workers in Lampang.
(c) The same 20 products are priced at a supermarket and at a fresh market.
(d) 30 firms that adopted a new technology are compared with 30 other firms that did not.

::: {.answer title="Exercise 3.3.1"}
(a) Paired (same families twice). (b) Independent (two separate samples).
(c) Paired (same products at two places). (d) Independent (different firms).
:::

**3.3.2** A consumer group priced the same `r length(shopA)` products at Shop A and
Shop B. It wants to know whether prices at Shop A are lower
on average. Use the output to write the decision and interpretation at
$\alpha$ = 0.05.

```{r}
#| label: r-data-shops
#| echo: !expr show_code
#| code: !expr c(vec_code("shopA", shopA), vec_code("shopB", shopB))
```

```{r}
#| label: r-ex-3-3
#| echo: !expr show_code
t.test(shopA, shopB, paired = TRUE, alternative = "less")
```

::: {.answer title="Exercise 3.3.2"}
$H_0: \mu_d = 0 \quad H_1: \mu_d < 0$ ($d$ = Shop A $-$ Shop B).
$t_{\text{cal}} = `r fmt(eo$statistic, 3)`$, df = `r eo$parameter`, p-value = `r fmt(eo$p.value, 4)`.
p-value = `r fmt(eo$p.value, 4)` < $\alpha$ = 0.05, so we reject $H_0$. That is,
prices at Shop A are lower than at Shop B on average at the 0.05 level of significance.
:::
